title: Safety Stock-Led Onboard Capacity Calculator
summary: Working spreadsheet to estimate required GPU safety stock and KV cache priming footprint for incremental model rollouts. Focuses on a statistic-driven safety-stock approach (target availability percentile) rather than ad-hoc slot reservations.
purpose: Provide SRE and capacity planning a compact calculator that converts model traffic forecasts + KV footprint profiles into a recommended initial safety-stock reservation per region and a phased KV priming plan with expected eviction headroom.
key_assumptions: Forecast horizon: first 6 weeks after public rollout
Traffic growth modeled as base QPS with log-normal daily variance (sigma tunable)
KV footprint = average active context bytes per model * active sessions estimate
Per-GPU available KV capacity is calibrated from recent fleet profiling (default 120GB usable per A100-like host for multi-tenant cache)
We prefer soft safety stock (pre-warmed spare GPUs) equal to Xth percentile of surge demand, not hard 100% over-provision
methodology: 1) Convert expected_peak_qps and active_session_ratio into active concurrent sessions. 2) Multiply by avg_context_bytes to get total KV bytes needed. 3) Apply traffic variance: safety_bytes = percentile(total_kv_bytes, target_percentile) using log-normal parameters derived from traffic_variance_sigma. 4) Safety_stock_gpus = ceil((safety_bytes - already_allocated_kv_bytes) / gpu_usable_kv_bytes). 5) Cross-check slot capacity: ensure slot_throughput_qps * (allocated_gpus - safety_stock_gpus) >= expected_peak_qps. If not, add compute-only GPUs (no significant KV) or throttle onset.
formulas_reference: concurrent_sessions = expected_peak_qps * avg_tokens_per_request / (avg_tokens_per_request) * active_session_ratio  (simplified to expected_peak_qps * active_session_ratio)
safety_bytes = exp( ln(total_kv_bytes) + z * sigma )  where z is the standard normal quantile for chosen percentile
scenarios: Conservative (95th percentile): large safety stock, slower rollout but low risk of eviction and p99 spikes
Balanced (90th percentile): medium safety stock, moderate cost with operational headroom
Aggressive (80th percentile): low upfront cost, requires fast KV priming and close monitoring
example_output_tables: Region | Allocated GPUs | Safety Stock GPUs | Priming Batches | Time to full warm (mins) | Expected eviction headroom GB
recommended_rollout_schedule: Week 0: 10% of traffic to canary with seeded priming (parallel priming to reach ~60% of steady-state KV). Week 1: increase to 30% if eviction <5% and p95 latency within target. Week 2: 60%. Week 4: full. Safety stock is released gradually after 4 weeks or after sustained lower variance for 7 days.
operational_triggers: If cache eviction > 8% during priming -> pause additional traffic and increase safety stock by 1 GPU in that region
If p99 latency exceeds target by >20% for 3 consecutive 5-minute windows -> divert new requests to fallback model variants
If GPU memory pressure consistently above 85% across >3 hosts -> schedule immediate scale-up event (add GPUs)
open_questions: What conservative default percentile should we pick for enterprise customers with SLA? (90/95?)
Should we bake in cross-region spill capacity automatically, or require manual ops approval for spill-over?
Can we implement a fast cold-start priming path that prioritizes top-k frequent prefixes to reduce initial KV bytes needed?
notes_to_self: Need to validate per-GPU usable KV bytes for newer instance types (H100 variants) and add a toggle for quantized KV footprints when using 8-bit caches. Also add a column for 'sticky sessions fraction' if rollout uses session affinity.
references: Onboard priming experiment results - run id: priming-2025-11
next_steps: 1) Run this sheet against last 3 months of traffic for model X and produce recommended safety_stock per region. 2) Pair with SRE to rehearse priming flow in staging. 3) Push a small dashboard for eviction and p99 alerts to Console as 'rollout health' dashboard.
audience: SREs, Infra planners, Solutions engineering, Product launch owners
